The Modified Camassa-Holm Equation: Wave breaking, Classification of Traveling Waves and Explicit Elliptic Peakons.

Journal: ??????????????????????
ALISSON DARÓS Address: Department of Mathematics, Federal University of Pampa, 97650-000 Itaqui, Brazil. alissondaros@unipampa.edu.br    LYNNYNGS KELLY ARRUDA SARAIVA DE PAIVA Address: Department of Mathematics, Federal University of São Carlos, PO B 676, 13565-905 São Carlos, Brazil. lynnyngs@dm.ufscar.br
Abstract

We show that wave breaking occurs for the modified Camassa-Holm (mCH) equation. Next we classify all traveling wave solutions of the modified Camassa-Holm equation in the weak sense via parametrization of their maxima, minima and wave velocity constants. This equation is shown to admit in addition to more popular solutions like smooth traveling waves and peakons, some not so well-known traveling waves as, for example, kinks, cuspons, composite waves and stumpons. Moreover, explicit peakons in terms of Jacobian elliptic functions are found.

Keywords: Wave breaking, peakons and global weak solutions.

1 Introduction

The original Camassa-Holm equation was introduced by Fuchssteiner and Fokas [12] through the method of recursion operators in 1981 and derived from physical principles by Camassa and Holm in 1999 [3].

Our purpose is to investigate the modified Camassa-Holm equation (mCH)

ut−ux​x​t=u​ux​x​x+2​ux​ux​x−3​u2​ux,x∈ℝ,t>0\displaystyle u_{t}-u_{xxt}=uu_{xxx}+2u_{x}u_{xx}-3u^{2}u_{x},\ \ x\in\mathbb{R},\ t>0 (1)
u​(x,0)=u0​(x),\displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x), (2)

obtained from modified Dullin-Gottwald-Holm (mDGH) equation [21]

u~t+κ​u~x−u~x​x​t−κ​u~x​x​x=u~​u~x​x​x+2​u~x​u~x​x−3​u~2​u~x,x∈ℝ,t>0,\tilde{u}_{t}+\kappa\tilde{u}_{x}-\tilde{u}_{xxt}-\kappa\tilde{u}_{xxx}=\tilde{u}\tilde{u}_{xxx}+2\tilde{u}_{x}\tilde{u}_{xx}-3\tilde{u}^{2}\tilde{u}_{x},\ \ x\in\mathbb{R},\ t>0,

by transformation u⁡(x,t)↦u~​(x+κ​t,t)u(x,t)\mapsto\tilde{u}(x+\kappa t,t). The original DGH equation was obtained by Dullin, Gottwald and Holm [11] for a unidirectional water wave with fluid velocity u⁡(x,t)u(x,t), where the constant κ≠0\kappa\neq 0 is the linear wave speed for undisturbed water at rest at spatial infinity.

The mCH equation can also be obtained from the a​bab-family of equations [14, 15, 16]

ut+(a(u))x−ux​x​t=(b′(u)ux22+b(u)ux​x)xu_{t}+(a(u))_{x}-u_{xxt}=\left(b^{{}^{\prime}}(u)\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{2}+b(u)u_{xx}\right)_{x} (3)

where a,b:ℝ⟶ℝa,b:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} are smooth function and a⁡(0)=0a(0)=0, by considering a⁡(u)=u3a(u)=u^{3} and b⁡(u)=ub(u)=u. From [14, 16] it is also known that (1) has three natural invariants:

E(u)=−∫ℝ[u48+u​ux22]dx,F(u)=12∫ℝ[u2+ux2]dxandV(u)=∫ℝudx.E(u)=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}\left[\frac{u^{4}}{8}+\frac{uu_{x}^{2}}{2}\right]\ dx,\ \ F(u)=\frac{1}{2}\int_{\mathbb{R}}[u^{2}+u_{x}^{2}]\ dx\ \ \ \text{and}\ \ \ V(u)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}u\ dx. (4)

Equation (1) has been investigated in recent years. Tian and Song in [24] obtained peakons composed of hyperbolic functions. In [25, 26], Wazwaz employed this modified form with k=0k=0 as a vehicle to explore the change in the physical structure of the solution from peakons to bell-shaped solitary wave solutions and showed that mCH equation has a s​e​c​hsec\ h like solitary wave solution. In [27], a variational homotopy perturbation method (VHPM) has been studied to obtain solitary wave solutions of the mCH equation. More recently in [7], we guarantee results about the orbital instability for a specific class of periodic traveling wave solutions with the mean zero property and large spatial period.

In this paper, we prove steepening at inflection points, i.e., we consider an initial condition in H3​(ℝ)H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) that has an inflection point to the right of its maximum and get that the time dependent slope at the inflection point becomes vertical in finite time. This property means that wave breaking holds. Next we classify all traveling wave solutions, u⁡(x,t)=ϕ⁡(x−c​t)u(x,t)=\phi(x-ct), c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R}, for mCH equation (1)(\ref{mCH}) using a weak formulation in Hl​o​c1​(ℝ)H^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}) and obtain explicit formulas for peakons in terms of Jacobian elliptic functions. As for the mDP equation [9], we also obtain some very interesting types of solutions such as kinks, cuspons, composite waves and stumpons, in addition to the more familiar smooth waves and peakons. To get an idea: the composite waves are obtained by combining cuspons and peakons into new traveling waves and the waves called stumpons are obtained by inserting intervals where ϕ\phi equals a constant at the crests of suitable cusped waves.

In the course of this work, we denote ⋆\star the convolution on ℝ\mathbb{R}. We also use (⋅,⋅)(\cdot,\cdot) to represent the standard inner product in Lp​e​r2​(ℝ)L^{2}_{per}(\mathbb{R}). For 1≤p≤∞1\leq p\leq\infty, the norm in the Lp​e​rp​(ℝ)L^{p}_{per}(\mathbb{R}) will be denoted by ||⋅||Lp||\cdot||_{L^{p}}, while ||⋅||s||\cdot||_{s} will stand for the norm in the classical Sobolev spaces Hp​e​rs​(ℝ)H^{s}_{per}(\mathbb{R}) for s≥0s\geq 0.

2 Preliminaries

Formally, problem (1)-(2) is equivalent to the hyperbolic-elliptic system

ut+∂x(u22)+Px=0,(x,t)∈ℝ×ℝ+,\displaystyle u_{t}+\partial_{x}\left(\frac{u^{2}}{2}\right)+P_{x}=0,\ \ (x,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}, (5)
P−Px​x=u3+u22+ux22,(x,t)∈ℝ×ℝ+,\displaystyle P-P_{xx}=u^{3}+\frac{u^{2}}{2}+\frac{{u_{x}}^{2}}{2},\ \ (x,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}, (6)
u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈ℝ\displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\ \ x\in\mathbb{R} (7)

The operator (1−∂x​x2)−1(1-\partial_{xx}^{2})^{-1} has a convolution structure:

(1−∂x​x2)−1(f)(x)=(G⋆f)(x),(1-\partial_{xx}^{2})^{-1}(f)(x)=(G\star f)(x), (8)

where G⁡(x)G(x) is the Green function

G⁡(x)=e−|x|2,x∈ℝ.\displaystyle G(x)=\frac{e^{-|x|}}{2},\ \ x\in\mathbb{R}.

Hence we have

P⁡(x,t)=G⋆(u3+u22+ux22)​(x,t),\displaystyle P(x,t)=G\star\left(u^{3}+\frac{u^{2}}{2}+\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{2}\right)(x,t), (9)

ut+F​(u)x=0,(x,t)∈ℝ×ℝ+,\displaystyle u_{t}+F(u)_{x}=0,\ \ (x,t)\in\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{+}, (10)
u⁡(x,0)=u0​(x),x∈ℝ,\displaystyle u(x,0)=u_{0}(x),\ \ x\in\mathbb{R}, (11)

where F⁡(u)=u22+G⋆(u3+u22+ux22)F(u)=\frac{u^{2}}{2}+G\star(u^{3}+\frac{u^{2}}{2}+\frac{u_{x}^{2}}{2}).

∫0T∫ℝ(u​ψt+F⁡(u)​ψx)​𝑑x​𝑑t+∫ℝu0​(x)​ψ0​(x)​𝑑x=0\int_{0}^{T}\int_{\mathbb{R}}(u\psi_{t}+F(u)\psi_{x})dxdt+\int_{\mathbb{R}}u_{0}(x)\psi_{0}(x)dx=0

3 Steepening lemma

The local well posedness of the Cauchy problem of Equation (1) with initial data u0∈Hs​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}), s>32s>\frac{3}{2} can be obtained by applying Kato’s semigroup theory [17]. More precisely, we have the following well-posedness result.

Theorem 1.

Given u0∈Hs​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{s}(\mathbb{R}), s>32s>\frac{3}{2}, there exists a maximal t0>0t_{0}>0 and a unique solution u⁡(x,t)u(x,t) to problem (1)-(2) such that

u∈C⁡([0,t0),Hs​(ℝ))∩C1​([0,t0),Hs−1​(ℝ)).u\in C([0,t_{0}),H^{s}(\mathbb{R}))\cap C^{1}([0,t_{0}),H^{s-1}(\mathbb{R})).

Moreover, the solution depends continuously on the initial data. For u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) the solution posseses the aditional regularity

u∈C⁡([0,t0),H3​(ℝ))∩C1​([0,t0),H2​(ℝ)).u\in C([0,t_{0}),H^{3}(\mathbb{R}))\cap C^{1}([0,t_{0}),H^{2}(\mathbb{R})).
Proof.

See Hakkaev, Iliev and Kirchev in [16]. ∎

Remark 1.

The solutions obtained in Theorem 1 are called strong solutions to Equation (1).

Assume now that u0∈H3​(ℝ)u_{0}\in H^{3}(\mathbb{R}) and let u∈C⁡([0,t0),H3​(ℝ))∩C1​([0,t0),H2​(ℝ))u\in C([0,t_{0});H^{3}(\mathbb{R}))\cap C^{1}([0,t_{0});H^{2}(\mathbb{R})) be the corresponding strong solution of (1)-(2).

4 Weak formulation

For a traveling wave u⁡(x,t)=ϕ⁡(ξ)u(x,t)=\phi(\xi), with ξ=x−c​t\xi=x-ct, the equation (1) is equivalent to

−cϕ′+cϕ′′′=ϕϕ′′′+2ϕ′ϕ′′−3ϕ2ϕ′,-c\phi^{{}^{\prime}}+c\phi^{{}^{\prime\prime\prime}}=\phi\phi^{{}^{\prime\prime\prime}}+2\phi^{{}^{\prime}}\phi^{{}^{\prime\prime}}-3\phi^{2}\phi^{{}^{\prime}}, (18)

where ′ denotes the derivative with respect to the variable ξ\xi.

After an integration with respect to the variable ξ\xi we can rewrite (18) as follows

(ϕ′)2+2ϕ3−2cϕ=((ϕ−c)2)′′+a.(\phi^{{}^{\prime}})^{2}+2\phi^{3}-2c\phi=((\phi-c)^{2})^{{}^{\prime\prime}}+a. (19)

for some constant of integration a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}. We see that for (19) to make any sense it is sufficient to require ϕ∈Hl​o​c1​(ℝ)\phi\in H^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}). Thus, the following definition is plausible.

Definition 2.

A function ϕ∈Hl​o​c1​(ℝ)\phi\in H^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}) is a traveling wave of the mCH equation if ϕ\phi satisfies (19) in distribution sense for some a∈ℝa\in\mathbb{R}.

5 Classification of traveling waves

Theorems 2 and 3 classify all bounded traveling waves ϕ∈Hl​o​c1​(ℝ)\phi\in H^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}), of (1). The bounded traveling waves are parametrized by their maxima, minima and speeds of propagation.

Theorem 2.

Consider z∈ℂ∖ℝz\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R} such that ℜ(z)=−(m+M)/2\Re(z)=-(m+M)/2 satisfying the equation m2+M2−|z|2+m​M−2​c=0m^{2}+M^{2}-|z|^{2}+mM-2c=0. Any bounded traveling wave of the mCH equation belongs to one of the following categories:

(a)(a) Smooth periodic: If m<M<cm<M<c, there is a smooth periodic traveling wave ϕ⁡(x−c​t)\phi(x-ct) of (1) with m=minξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi) and M=maxξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)M=\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi).

(b)(b) Periodic peakons: If m<M=cm<M=c, there is a periodic peaked traveling wave ϕ⁡(x−c​t)\phi(x-ct) of (1) with m=minξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi) and M=maxξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)M=\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi).

(c)(c) Periodic cuspons: If m<c<Mm<c<M, there is a periodic cusped traveling wave ϕ⁡(x−c​t)\phi(x-ct) of (1) with m=minξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi) and c=maxξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)c=\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi).

(a′)(a^{{}^{\prime}}) Smooth periodic: If c<M<mc<M<m, there is a smooth periodic traveling wave ϕ⁡(x−c​t)\phi(x-ct) of (1) with M=minξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)M=\min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi) and m=maxξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi).

(b′)(b^{{}^{\prime}}) Periodic peakons: If c=M<mc=M<m, there is a periodic peaked traveling wave ϕ⁡(x−c​t)\phi(x-ct) of (1) with M=minξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)M=\min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi) and m=maxξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi).

(c′)(c^{{}^{\prime}}) Periodic cuspons: If M<c<mM<c<m, there is a periodic cusped traveling wave ϕ⁡(x−c​t)\phi(x-ct) of (1) with c=minξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)c=\min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi) and m=maxξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi).

(d)(d) Composite waves: For each c∈ℝc\in\mathbb{R} fixed, with c<0c<0, consider the equation

2​a=(M+m)​(|z|2−m​M)2a=(M+m)(|z|^{2}-mM) (20)

in space (m,M,ℑ⁡(z))(m,M,\Im(z)) with z∈ℂ∖ℝz\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R} satisfying, less than a change of variables, the hyperboloid of two sheet

m2α2−M2β2−ℑ⁡(z)2γ2=1,\frac{m^{2}}{\alpha^{2}}-\frac{M^{2}}{\beta^{2}}-\frac{\Im(z)^{2}}{\gamma^{2}}=1, (21)

where α=−2​c\alpha=\sqrt{-2c}, β=2​−c\beta=2\sqrt{-c} and γ=−c\gamma=\sqrt{-c}. For any (m,M,c)(m,M,c) ∈{m<c⩽M}∪{m>c⩾M}\in\{m<c\leqslant M\}\cup\{m>c\geqslant M\} there is a corresponding cuspon or peakon according to (b)(b) or (c)(c) and (b′)(b^{{}^{\prime}}) or (c′)(c^{{}^{\prime}}). A countable number of cuspons and peakons corresponding to points (m,M,c)(m,M,c) that belong to the same hyperboloid of two sheet, may be joined at their crests to form a composite wave ϕ\phi. If the Lebesgue measure μ​(ϕ−1​(c))=0\mu(\phi^{-1}(c))=0, then ϕ\phi is a traveling wave of (1).

(e)(e) Stumpons: For a=2​c3−2​c2a=2c^{3}-2c^{2} the equation (20) jointly with (21) contains the points (m,M,ℑ⁡(z))=(c,c,±4​c2−2​c)(m,M,\Im(z))=(c,c,\pm\sqrt{4c^{2}-2c}). These equations correspond only to cuspons. Let ϕ\phi be a composite wave obtained by joining countably many of these cuspons with each other and with intervals where ϕ≡c\phi\equiv c. Then ϕ\phi is a traveling wave of (1) even if μ​(ϕ−1​(c))>0\mu(\phi^{-1}(c))>0.

Theorem 3.

Consider z=−m−r−Mz=-m-r-M with r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R} satisfying the equation r2+m2+M2+r​m+r​M+m​M−2​c=0r^{2}+m^{2}+M^{2}+rm+rM+mM-2c=0. Any bounded traveling wave of the mCH equation belongs, less than an alternation of zz for rr, to one of the following categories:

(a)(a) Smooth periodic: If z<r<m<M<cz<r<m<M<c, there is a smooth periodic traveling wave ϕ⁡(x−c​t)\phi(x-ct) of (1) with m=minξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi) and M=maxξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)M=\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi).

In addition to Theorems 2 and 3 is possible to characterize the existence or no of some unbounded traveling waves of the mCH equation.

Theorem 4.

If the polynomial P⁡(ϕ)P(\phi) in (35) has only a real zero, say mm, then the mCH equation has not bounded solutions ϕ\phi to c<mc<m or m<cm<c with m=minξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\min_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi) or m=maxξ∈ℝ⁡ϕ⁡(ξ)m=\max_{\xi\in\mathbb{R}}\phi(\xi), respectively. In particular, the mCH equation has traveling wave solutions with exponential behavior.

Remark 3.

Differently from the classical case, the mCH equation has not traveling wave solutions with similar behavior to a parabola because this is only possible if the polynomial P⁡(ϕ)P(\phi) in (35) has only a real zero with multiplicity equal to one.

To prove Theorems 2 and 3, we will show that the set of bounded functions satisfying (T​W​1)−(T​W​3)(TW1)-(TW3) in Lemma 5 consists exactly of the waves presented in the statements of these theorems.

Suppose that ϕ\phi satisfies (T​W​1)−(T​W​2)(TW1)-(TW2). From (T​W​1)(TW1) and (T​W​2)(TW2) there is a countable number of C∞C^{\infty} wave segments separated by a closed set CC such that each wave segment ϕ\phi satisfies

andϕ→c​at any finite endpoint of​E\displaystyle\text{and}\ \ \phi\rightarrow c\ \text{at any finite endpoint of}\ E (30)

for some interval EE and constants a,da,d. If we are able to find all solutions of (30)(\ref{184}) for different intervals EE and different values of aa and dd, then we can join solutions defined at intervals in which the union is ℝ∖C\mathbb{R}\setminus C for some closed set CC of null measure. We will have the function that we constructed defined in ℝ\mathbb{R}, satisfying (T​W​1)(TW1) and (T​W​2)(TW2) if, and only if, all the wave segments satisfy (30) with the same constant aa. In addition, if for a=2​c3−2​c2a=2c^{3}-2c^{2} we allow μ⁡(C)>0\mu(C)>0, this procedure will give us all the functions satisfying (T​W​1)(TW1) and (T​W​2)(TW2). To study (30), we first observe that for general equations of the form

ϕ(ξ)=m+14(ξ−η)2F′(m)+O((ξ−η)4)atξ↑η,\phi(\xi)=m+\frac{1}{4}(\xi-\eta)^{2}F^{{}^{\prime}}(m)+O((\xi-\eta)^{4})\ \ \text{at}\ \ \xi\uparrow\eta, (32)

If FF has a double zero mm, a simple zero MM, and F⁡(ϕ)>0F(\phi)>0 for m<ϕ<Mm<\phi<M, then there are solutions with decay. To FF with a simple zero at mm and F⁡(ϕ)>0F(\phi)>0 for m<ϕm<\phi, then no bounded solution ϕ\phi exists.

If we include all the functions ϕ∈Hl​o​c1​(ℝ)\phi\in H^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}) that are solutions of (31), we will expand the class of solutions, so that they will have another qualitative behavior. If ϕ\phi approaches a simple pole ϕ=c\phi=c of FF, then, if ϕ⁡(ξ0)=c\phi(\xi_{0})=c,

Suppose that there are two simple real zeros, say mm and MM, and we going to prove Theorem 2. We write for z∈ℂ∖ℝz\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R}

and comparing the coefficients of (35) we obtain that ℜ(z)=−(M+m)/2\Re(z)=-(M+m)/2 with z∈ℂ∖ℝz\in\mathbb{C}\setminus\mathbb{R} satisfying the hyperboloid of two sheet in (m,M,ℑ⁡(z))(m,M,\Im(z)),

and, from (32), we deduce from that there are periodic solutions C∞C^{\infty} for (30) if and only if m<M<cm<M<c or c<M<mc<M<m. Note that these solutions never touch the line ϕ=c\phi=c. Thus, the interval EE in (30) must be the whole real line. In particular, these C∞C^{\infty} solutions can never be glued together with another wave.

For the case of bounded solutions to (30) for which ϕ→c\phi\rightarrow c at a finite end-point of EE, gluing two of these together will give rise to a non-smooth wave. Periodic peakons occur if we leave m<M=cm<M=c. In fact, consider ϕ\phi a solution such that m⩽ϕ⩽Mm\leqslant\phi\leqslant M. If ϕ\phi is decreasing it will reach mm and turn back up to reaches MM. ϕ\phi can not stop or turn back anywhere because ϕ\phi has not singularities at points where ϕ≠c\phi\neq c. But note that ϕ\phi increases until reaches ϕ=c\phi=c and it can make a sudden turn at this point. This suddenly change of direction of ϕ\phi makes ϕ′\phi^{{}^{\prime}} have a jump which gives rise to a peak. To see how periodic cuspons happen, consider m<c<Mm<c<M. In this case, F⁡(ϕ)F(\phi) has a simple zero at mm, a simple pole at cc and F⁡(ϕ)>0F(\phi)>0 for m<ϕ<cm<\phi<c. Thus, from (34) we have

for some constant α\alpha. In particular, the solution ϕ\phi has a cusp.

These are all nontrivial bounded solutions of (30) for this distribution of zeros of the polynomial P⁡(ϕ)P(\phi) and correspond to items (a)−(c)(a)-(c) and (a′)−(c′)(a^{{}^{\prime}})-(c^{{}^{\prime}}) of Theorem 2.

where z=−m−r−Mz=-m-r-M and r∈ℝr\in\mathbb{R} satisfies equation (37)(\ref{elipsoide}). So, (37) can be rewrite in its reduced form

To finalize the proof of Theorems 2 and 3 is enough to show that these waves belong to Hl​o​c1​(ℝ)H^{1}_{loc}(\mathbb{R}) and satisfy (T​W​3)(TW3). This fact is ensured by Lemma 9 but in order to prove this lemma we need to establish some technical results and notation.

Definition 3.

A function f:I⟶ℝf:I\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}, I=[a,b]⊂ℝI=[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}, is said to be of bounded variation if

sup∑i=1N|f⁡(ti)−f⁡(ti−1)|<+∞,\sup\sum_{i=1}^{N}|f(t_{i})-f(t_{i-1})|<+\infty,

where the supremum is taken over all natural number NN and all choices of partitions {ti}i=1N\{t_{i}\}_{i=1}^{N} such that a=t0<t1<⋯<tN=ba=t_{0}<t_{1}<\cdot\cdot\cdot<t_{N}=b. B​V​(I)BV(I) denote the set of functions f:I⟶ℝf:I\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} of bounded variation on II. B​Vl​o​c​(ℝ)BV_{loc}(\mathbb{R}) denote the space of functions f:ℝ⟶ℝf:\mathbb{R}\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} of bounded variation for all compact intervals I⊂ℝI\subset\mathbb{R}.

Definition 4.

A function f:X⟶ℝf:X\longrightarrow\mathbb{R} defined on some set X⊂ℝX\subset\mathbb{R} is an NN-function if ff maps sets of measure zero to sets of measure zero.

Lemma 6.

A function f:I⟶ℝf:I\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}, I=[a,b]⊂ℝI=[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}, is absolutely continuous if and only if f∈Wl​o​c1,1​(I)f\in W^{1,1}_{loc}(I).

Lemma 7.

Let f:I⟶ℝf:I\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}, I=[a,b]⊂ℝI=[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}, be a continuous function of bounded variation. Then, ff is absolutely continuous if and only if ff is an NN-function.

Lemma 8.

If f:I⟶ℝf:I\longrightarrow\mathbb{R}, I=[a,b]⊂ℝI=[a,b]\subset\mathbb{R}, is continuous and |f||f| is absolutely continuous, the ff is absolutely continuous.

The proof of Lemmas 6−-8 can be found on book [22].

Remark 5.

In Theorems 2 and 3 the solutions are defined on the whole real line. Here we restrict the solution to the interval between two crests in the case of periodic waves, and to the part left or right of the crest in the case of decaying waves. The interval EE is accordingly defined to be a finite or half-infinite interval.

In addition to Theorems 2 and 3, it is possible to characterize the relation between the traveling waves of (1) and the parameters mm, MM and cc. Namely, such traveling waves are continuously dependents on these parameters.

10 Appendix

In this appendix we will talk about some concepts used so far without further explanation. In accordance with [2], we start setting the normal elliptic integral of the first kind

F⁡(ϕ,k)=F⁡(ϕ|k2)=Fk​(ϕ)=∫0yd​t(1−t2)​(1−k2​t2)=∫0ϕd​φ(1−k2​sin2⁡φ),F(\phi,k)=F(\phi\ |\ k^{2})=F_{k}(\phi)=\int_{0}^{y}\ \frac{dt}{\sqrt{(1-t^{2})(1-k^{2}t^{2})}}=\int_{0}^{\phi}\frac{d\varphi}{\sqrt{(1-k^{2}\sin^{2}\varphi)}},

where y=sin⁡ϕy=\sin\phi.

The parameter kk is called the modulus of the elliptic integral and k′2=1−k2k^{\prime 2}=1-k^{2} its complementary modulus, and both may take any real or imaginary value. Here we wish to take 0<k2<10<k^{2}<1. Moreover, the variable ϕ\phi is called argument and it is usually taken belonging to [−π2,π2]\left[\frac{-\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right].

In his algebraic form, the elliptic integral above is finite for all real (or complex) values of yy, including infinity. When ϕ=π2\phi=\frac{\pi}{2}, the integral K⁡(k)​=˙​F​(π2,k)K(k)\dot{=}F\left(\frac{\pi}{2},k\right) is said to be complete.

We define the Jacobian elliptic functions using the inverse function of the elliptic integral of the first kind. This inverse function exists because that

u⁡(y1,k)≡u=∫0y1d​t(1−t2)​(1−k2​t2)=∫0ϕd​φ1−k2​sin2⁡φ=F⁡(ϕ,k),u(y_{1},k)\equiv u=\int_{0}^{y_{1}}\frac{dt}{\sqrt{(1-t^{2})(1-k^{2}t^{2})}}=\int_{0}^{\phi}\frac{d\varphi}{\sqrt{1-k^{2}\sin^{2}\varphi}}=F(\phi,k),

is a strictly increasing function of the real variable y1y_{1} and, in its algebraic form, this integral has the property of being finite for all values of y1y_{1}. This inverse ϕ=am⁡(u,k)=am​u\phi=\mathrm{am}(u,k)=\mathrm{am}u is called amplitude function.

There are several Jacobian elliptic functions that can be seen in [2], but here we will only define the functions sn, cn and tn as follows

sn​(u,k)=sin​am​(u,k)=sin​ϕ,cn​(u,k)=cos​am​(u,k)=cos​ϕ,tn​(u,k)=sin​am​(u,k)cos​am​(u,k)=sin​ϕcos​ϕ.\begin{array}[]{lll}\text{sn}(u,k)=\text{sin}\ \mathrm{am}(u,k)=\text{sin}\phi,&&\\ \text{cn}(u,k)=\text{cos}\ \mathrm{am}(u,k)=\text{cos}\phi,&&\\ \text{tn}(u,k)=\displaystyle\frac{\text{sin}\ \mathrm{am}(u,k)}{\text{cos}\ \mathrm{am}(u,k)}=\frac{\text{sin}\phi}{\text{cos}\phi}.&&\end{array}

These functions have a real period, namely 4​K​(k)4K(k), and some important properties summarized by the formulas given below.

sn​(−u)=−sn​(u),sn2​u+cn2​u=1,cn​(−u)=cn​(u),−1⩽snu,cnu⩽1,tn​(−u)=−tn​(u),sn​(i​u,k)=i​tn​(u,k′).\begin{array}[]{lll}\text{sn}(-u)=-\text{sn}(u),&&\ \ \text{sn}^{2}u+\text{cn}^{2}u=1,\\ \text{cn}(-u)=\text{cn}(u),&&\ \ -1\leqslant\text{sn}u,\text{cn}u\leqslant 1,\\ \text{tn}(-u)=-\text{tn}(u),&&\ \ \text{sn}(iu,k)=i\text{tn}(u,k^{\prime}).\end{array}
